utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution Alexis Demirdjian; assisted by Crispian Smith, our case manager; and Mr. Tom Hannis, Senior Trial Attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing that need delay us, would the usher please escort the witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you please give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Good morning, sir. What is your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Vidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 27th of August, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And your profession, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to work in prison, and I'm a teacher by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever testify before for this Tribunal or for a court in your country about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not here. As for my country, there was some divorce case, and there was some squabble about a flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But not to do with the matters that we deal with here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Vidic, as a witness for the Prosecution, the Prosecutor will start asking questions. After the Prosecutor, the -- both of the Defence teams, on that side, will cross-examine you. And there will be re-direct examination, eventually new questions from the Prosecutor. And after that, eventually the Judges could have some questions for you. We sit by half a day's hearing; that is, from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00; or, in the afternoon, from a quarter past 2.00 to 7.00. That's a long time. But there will be -- normally, there will be breaks every, more or less, one hour and a half. There will be a 20 minutes' break. That's necessary for all kinds of reasons, interpreters, the tapes, for the record, et cetera. If you feel any problem and you're tired -- you need -- you need to have a small break and a rest, please tell us, and we will accommodate you. You understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis. Im sorry, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend Mr. Demirdjian. Just I would like to put on the record objection of the Defence. This witness gave interview on the 24th of November, 2009, and in the presence of Mr. Demirdjian on the question of investigator Michael Koehler, and I will quote his -- Mr. Koehler's statement to this witness: "Based upon information in possession of the Tribunal, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal believed you may be a suspect who is responsible for committing acts by may chargeable under the Tribunal statute. However, the ICTY is not going to prosecute you or investigate you in regard to these suspected acts. Do you understand?" And Mr. Vidic answer was yes. Just for the record, Your Honours, it is a practice which is absolutely unacceptable from the point of view of the Defence, practice of the Prosecution, and the -- we raised that issue on many occasions before. I don't want to raise that issue to discuss, but just to put on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed this is a matter that has been raised many times before. I don't understand why Mr. Pantelic finds it necessary to put it on the record in front of this witness, at this time. If he wants to have further discussion about it, we can have the witness removed. But we have explained why the Prosecution, pursuant to the rules, made these kinds of advices to witnesses in that position. There is no purpose in serving this expect to cause some kind of disturbance to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is totally unacceptable statement of my friend Mr. Hannis, and we know that OTP is not entitled to conduct any investigation due to the exit strategy of the Tribunal, and in spite of this fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if this is a matter which requires serious exploration, and as both you and Mr. Hannis have said this is a matter that has been raised before, then perhaps we should do it in the proper manner, but certainly not in the presence of the witness. So unless there is some good reason for not proceeding with the examination of this witness, we would suspend any further discussion of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I begin, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidic. I apologise for that introduction but I will begin with my questions. You already stated your name and your date of birth. Could you tell the Trial Chamber about your educational background, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I finished the faculty of industrial pedagogy, and I am the professor of mechanics and technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what year did you finish your studies?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what level of studies did you achieve?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Bachelor of arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct to say that after university you worked in a prison, Goli Otok, between the years 1977 and 1979 in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And your role there was an educator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. I worked there as an educator. But since the correction facility had its own school, I also worked part-time as a teacher there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Is it correct that after two years in Goli Otok you went do Doboj where you were teaching for four months in a school of mechanical engineering?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is correct to say that on the 1st of April 1980 you were employed and hired by the Doboj Central Prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber which year you retired?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you were hired in 1980, what were you hired as? What was your position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: An educator.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber what your role consisted of as an educator.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I worked in the district prison as a person who receives the convicts and through whom the convicts exercise their rights and, at the same time, try to rehabilitate, in terms of me instructing them to maintain contacts with their families, if these were disruptive families, and in that manner sort of prepare them for the time when they are released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you held on to this position until the outbreak of the conflict in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the structure of the prison. Can you, first of all, tell us, in relation to the Doboj Central Prison, what type of prison it was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It was a district prison, according to the categorisation of correctional and prison facility in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was a closed type facility. Remand custody and normal imprisonment, up to six months were carried out in that prison. The minister, or rather, the secretary at the time, was entitled to distribute the convicts. Sometimes it happened that serving prison sentence were people who were sentenced to more than six months of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us what type of prison it was and what type of prisoners were held there. Could you explain to us the structure of the prison, in terms of management positions. Who would we see at the top levels of the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The governor was at the head of the prison. Then there were heads of services.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just a clarification here. The governor was at the head of the prison. What did you mean by the governor?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It's a British word for warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. It has been clarified now on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What are the different services inside of the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was the guard service, the rehabilitation service, the legal and administrative and personnel service, and the economic unit. As part of the administrative and legal service was the medical unit and the financial unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the economic unit. Could you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The economic service was in charge of conducting labour therapy for the convicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did this economic unit, was it known by another name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Spreca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was this unit held in the same facility as the prison, in the same building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. It was dislocated, some 3 kilometres from the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the capacity of the prison, in terms of numbers of convicts and detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There were certain quotas which says that each convict is entitled to four square metres or eight cubic metres of space. However, when asked about the capacity, one of my former wardens said, Nobody was sent back due to the lack of space. So according to the present standards in place, the capacity for serving sentences and for custody is about 100 persons in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to come back to an answer you gave earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. 8, 4/5, I believe the witness says, No one was sent due to lack of space.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is what I heard as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, just to clarify an answer you provided us earlier you mentioned that the economic unit was also known as Spreca. When we talk about Spreca we only refer to that economic unit that was 3 kilometres away from the prison building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in due course, I will make some applications because the adjudicated facts may have some confusion about what the prison was called exactly. But that is a point I will raise in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vidic, where was the prison situated in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It was on the main street now called St. Sava Street, formally called Marshal Tito Street. But I'm not sure about the number. It is either 12 or 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say that it was in the main street in terms of the town itself, how would you locate the prison? In which parts of town was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It's in down-town, the very centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What building were adjacent -- what buildings were adjacent to the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was a bank, a MUP building, a court building, the prosecutor's office. Those are the adjacent buildings. Behind, were residential houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While I'm asking the next question, perhaps 65 ter 3419.29 could be pulled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, was the prison connected to any other building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Since it was built sometime in 1986 or 1987, it was connected to the court-house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we saw this map yesterday, but I will ask different questions about it. With the help of the usher, perhaps, if the witness could mark this aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Vidic, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Very quickly with the letter A, if you could just mark the prison building for us.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that it was connected to the court-house. Could you show us where that connection was. And mark it with a letter B.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you explain to us how it was connected to the court-house.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Up until 1986 or 1987, the court-house and the prosecutor's office were in one building, but a detached building. More due to the requirements of the court, they built a link with the prison building on the ground floor. That was the only connection. And in the section where these two buildings meet, a door was open, and the key to this door was only held by the prison personnel. It was used in the event of special security reasons when some people had to be escorted to the court. But as far as I know, it's never been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And below the building you marked with the letter B, there are two other buildings. Could you tell what these are.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. In front?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just -- well, on the image just below the building marked with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Connected to the building with the letter B, just below it, what was that building right there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Right. That's the court-house and the prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the letter C.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we could seize that image, I'd like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, I'd like to turn on to the record-keeping in the prison. Could you explain to the Court how would the prison record every prisoner serving a sentence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The prescribed records of convicts were kept in the form of a register; the birth and deaths register, and the personal file of the convict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would such a record also include the decision upon which the convict was ordered to be detained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: In order for a convict to be admitted to serve their sentence, before the convict shows up at the prison, the court has to send the prison an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to these records, was there also a record for detainees, non-convicted persons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, according to the procedure, according to the law, how long could a detainee be held in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Sentences up to six months. I'm not sure, in fact. I told you, I worked as an educator, and the remand prison was managed by the head of the guard service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, maybe my question was not clear. I was talking about the detainees; people who were detained not convicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness -- the witness answered properly to your question. It is just -- it was recorded. But I don't have my the phones on -- earphone off -- on, so I don't know what was translated. But he was actually referring to the detention not sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On -- could you clarify, Mr. Vidic, on whose -- you told us that you would need a court's order to detain someone. How would that order come to the prison? How would it reach you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Well, that depends who was sending a person. It could be the MUP. The MUP could detain a person in remand up to three days. Such orders were delivered by the MUP. For longer detention, the MUP would apply to the prosecutor's office, and the prosecutor's office would decide on a prolongation, or it could be the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the courts, what responsibility did the courts have over the well-being of prisoners inside the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: In fact, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me clarify it for you. Would the court be informed of the conditions in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was legislation stipulating the conditions that a correctional/penal facility had to provided and ensure, and there was nothing controversial about that. In regard to any problem with any detainee or prisoner, the prison was required to inform the competent court. In addition to that, the president of the district court had a duty to visit the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How often would the president of the court visit the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Perhaps once a month; perhaps more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, during -- if you're holding a detainee, and that this detainee is under investigation, were there premises in the prison for visits and interviews?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if a detainee was to be interviewed, would it normally take place in the prison, or would it take place elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: In the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could a detainee be taken out of the prison for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. On orders of the court, or whoever detained him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was the procedure to have an interview with a detainee outside the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The court would issue a warrant for a detainee to be taken out, and the guard would lead him out. That would be mostly to the court-house or, if a detainee had health problems, he would be taken to the health centre or the hospital; but, again, with the approval of the court. Without the approval of the court, it was impossible to take anyone out of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If the police wished to interview a detainee, would it also need a court order?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was there a difference for convicts and detainees in the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was. It was the prison administration who was responsible for convicts. As far as remand was concerned, the administration of the prison was just servicing the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if the police wished to interview a -- a person on remand, would it to have to go through the court?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: If it was remand in custody up to three days, that was in the competence of the police, the MUP. So the MUP did not need anyone's approval. If it was longer for -- than three days, then the court had to give approval to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just briefly, if could you explain the procedure for someone who is in detention up to three days, what would the procedure for the police to take out the detainee and interrogate or interview him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: They would bring a warrant from the MUP, properly phrased and signed, and submit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to turn reporting. Who would the prison warden be responsible to, who would he report to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: In those times, to the secretariat and the republican secretary for justice. Now it is called ministry and minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was the warden duty-bound to send periodical reports to the ministry or to the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The warden was duty-bound to send annual reports. In addition to that, he was duty-bound to inform the secretariat about any and all changes occurring, such as injuries to prisoners, the use of force, epidemics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: With regard to the use of force, could you expand on that. Would that be reported to the ministry annually, or would that be on another occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: That was reported immediately to the ministry, by telephone, as soon as it was found out. And then after all the information was collected, a written report would be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what procedure was in place in the situation where force was applied against a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: As soon as information was received on application of force, the guard would report it to the warden, and the warden would start disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, could we just clarify which ministry we're talking about. Is it the Ministry of Justice or the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: He answered it earlier, but I can clarify again if you wish. He said Secretariat for justice at page 14, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think it is still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, you just explained how the procedure would take place. You said the warden would start disciplinary proceedings. Could you expand on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Based on any information collected by a head of the service, the head of service would submit all the information to the warden, and the warden would then decide if there were the necessary elements to start disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Who would be involved in the disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was a disciplinary commission made up of prison employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was there anybody from other institutions that would be involved, or is it only prison employees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Only prison employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Over and above disciplinary measures, could criminal measures be applied?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: We did not have such a case, but the possibility existed. If there were the required elements, a criminal report could be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who would be involved in preparing this criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The legal officer from the legal and administrative service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who would he send this report to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, we didn't have such a case, but I suppose to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to the records of the prison you mentioned earlier, could you tell us within the prison who maintained the records: One for the records of convicts; and, two, records for persons on remand.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The register for detainees on remand were kept by the head of the guard service. And the register of convicts was kept by the officer in charge of execution of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there a duty officer at the entrance of the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did he maintain a log-book?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: He kept a duty log-book. Duty service log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, what would be included in this log-book?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Who was admitted for serving a sentence, who was admitted for custody and remand, who was released from detention. Any and all important observations would be entered by the duty officer during his tour of duty, because the guard service worked 20 hours a day. And in the absence of the warden, which means after normal working hours, the duty officer at the prison was responsible for the establishment of the prison and who stands in for the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, I would like now to turn to the events in 1991 and 1992. First of all, if you could tell the Court during the multi-party elections, did you personally join any political party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after the elections, did you, at any time, join any political party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In 1991, you were still in your role -- in your position as an educator; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In 1991, who was the prison warden?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: We had an acting warden at the time, Mirko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the same time, he was head of the guard service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, the last name of the warden was not recorded on the transcript. Would you just repeat his last name, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Mirko Slavuljica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe -- you should ask the witness again to repeat, because -- just the last name. It is in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While I'm asking the next question, we could pull up 65 ter 3528, please. Mr. Vidic, you told us that Mr. Slavuljica was the acting warden. Could you just explain to us the "acting."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It was some kind of provisional measure, pending the appointment of a new warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now can you see the document on the screen. This is a document that I've shown you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S version. And that would be page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Mirko Slavuljica's.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And it -- what is the title? It reads there, indeed, that he is acting prison warden. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go back to the top of the document, and that's page 1 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us under what circumstances this document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Mirko was a reserve officer, and he had received a call-up into the reserve from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And by this document, what functions and what role are attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I was put in charge of performing the duties of a -- of the warden and making sure that the establishment is run properly. This was kind of a forced decision, because in the job staffing specification there is no such position as deputy warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time, you had you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, after Mr. Slavuljica was called up to the army reserve, was he still present at the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: He would come by from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was he still fulfilling his functions as warden or acting warden?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "from time to time," could you just give the Trial Chamber of how frequently he would be at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It would be pure speculation now, after all this time. But he came by -- he's a responsible kind of person, and he cared a lot to have the institution run properly, so he did spend -- spend a lot of time with us, despite the fact that he was in the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In 1991, how many staff members did you have in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to be precise about that, but it was already a time when the whole state was in crisis and orders were coming from the secretariat to down-size. So how many staff we had in which period, I couldn't say for sure, but we had between 36 and 39 staff members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what was the ethnic makeup of your staff in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: You're asking too much. I really can't say. But I can say that we did take care to maintain an ethnic balance so that it be representative of the population. But since I wasn't directly responsible for that sort of work, I can't say whether our ethnic structure reflected the ethnic composition of the municipality or the region. But it was certainly proper ethnic representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you just explain to the Trial Chamber when you say "maintaining the ethnic balance," based on what did you maintain this balance, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Well, the ethnic composition of both the municipality and the region were known facts. And some time in 1991, although I'm telling you, I didn't have any involvement in such work directly, a medical technician was being hired, and it was said, at the time, that it had to be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, before I move on to the events in 1992, could you briefly explain to us how many meals per day would be provided to the prisoners inside the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Three meals. And convicts who worked, as it was stipulated by the law, received an additional fourth meal. But since it was not exactly stipulated what exactly constituted hard physical labour, this fourth meal was given to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you describe to the Court the uniform of the guards in your prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The uniform was dark blue, and the shirt was light blue, and the tie was of dark blue colour, and they had a hat on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How did this uniform compare to the regular uniform of the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The police had some sort of light greyish colour uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, we have adjudicated facts about the start of the conflict in early 1992, so I will skip to part and go straight to the events of May 1992, with your leave. Mr. Vidic, could you tell us when roughly you heard about the beginning of the conflict in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It was on or about the 3rd of May, in the morning. It could have been between 6.00 and 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How did you come to learn about it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Since it was a holiday, the 1st of May, I was at my father-in-law's summer cottage, and a colleague of mine, a guard, knew where the cottage was, and he came there and informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And where was the summer cottage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It was in the village of Strijezevica [phoen], 8 kilometres from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now what happened when your colleague informed you? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Well, I immediately went to the prison. There, I saw that this huge gate was open. And in the lounge, or in the hall, were people in camouflage uniforms and painted faces. I don't know at this moment, but I think I saw two or three guards as well, inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On your way from the summer cottage to the prison, did you notice anything specific?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I did not notice anything of the kind. Because it was a Sunday, it was holiday, it was pretty early in the morning, and due to all these factors, I didn't see or notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulty getting to the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you saw individuals in camouflage uniform and painted faces. How many of these individuals did you see?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. To me, it was a shock to see them there. Because this institution was of a strictly closed type, it was highly respected in the town. The gate was never opened, and, on that day, when I came, I see the gate wide open, and I see a lot of strangers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were these people armed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the situation inside the prison, when you see these men.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I tried to pass through as quickly as possible, pass by them and reach my office. There, I was told that three guards had been locked up by these men. I couldn't get any information from the employees of ours that I saw downstairs. So I went myself to see my colleagues in other offices because I heard that they sent a message asking to talk to me immediately. They asked me what was going on and what was happening, but I wasn't able to provide them with any answers. I gave all the cigarettes I have to the guard called Braderic, and I promised them that I would do my best to find with the MUP what this was all about and that I was going to notify Slavuljica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened to Braderic? Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: He was locked up in a cell, in the custody section of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was he the only guard to be in custody?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No, there were two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see other detainees in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There were very few detainees at the time, which is immediately before the war. Some amnesties were issued before the war which greatly affected the numbers. The numbers were drastically reduced. There were only a couple of people in prison serving sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on the 3rd of May, when you arrived at the prison, how many people were imprisoned there, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure, but there were no more than 15 of them, definitely. Both among those who were in custody and both among convicts serving their sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that you saw these individuals in camouflage uniform. Did you -- were you able to tell if they had a leader?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you spoke to Braderic; you gave him your cigarettes, and you would do your best to speak to the MUP and to notify Slavuljica. What, if anything, did you do about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to call Slavuljica, but I failed to establish a connection. Then I headed off towards MUP to find someone there, someone who -- who was a high-ranking official. Also, in this reception area in the MUP, there was also a large group of men in camouflage uniforms, and since the MUP management were on the upper storey, these men on the ground floor did not let me pass through. Therefore, I went back to prison, called Slavuljica again, and finally managed to get in touch with him sometime after 9.00. And Slavuljica came out relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When Slavuljica arrived at the prison, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: We first briefed him about the current situation, and he immediately went to the MUP. I don't know who he talked there to, and then, after that, he returned to us again. Our three officers were released from the cells, our three employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Slavuljica arrived, you said that you briefed him and he went to the MUP. Did you see those three guards released?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The custody cells are on the upper storey, and I saw them later in the ground floor offices. And I spent some time with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you if they were given any reasons for being put in those cells?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the MUP building you tried to go to, was this -- which MUP building were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was only one MUP building in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that is the one that you explained earlier was next to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time when you attempted to go to the MUP, did you have in mind someone specific you would like to meet?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. I thought to try and find the chief of the centre, the chief of the station, the chief of the criminal investigation police. Anyone of that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know these individuals at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I knew the chief of the centre. I saw him only once, though. As for the chief of the station, I didn't know him. I didn't even know who was at the head of the criminal investigation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that on that day you must have had, at most, 15 detainees. Did those numbers vary on that day and on the following days?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It started changing right from the start. On the 3rd of May, they started bringing people in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, maybe I missed it, but I would like you to clarify with the witness the reasons why he went to the MUP and -- and my question is really, did he do so because the wardens and the prison guards were employed by the MUP, were they MUP employees, or was it because the prison, as such, was run by the MUP? Or ... What was the purpose of going to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, you heard Your Honour's [sic] question. What was the purpose of going to the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I went to the MUP building because we were dealing with prison employees who had been on duty the previous night. The prison was never within the management system of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you're saying that the prison was never within the management system of the MUP. You clarified earlier that you were within the Ministry of Justice. Did you try to go to the court, perhaps, on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vidic, you were telling us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- interrupt. And perhaps I'm missing something, but I'm not clear on the relationship between the MUP, the prison, the Ministry of Justice. If could you assist me there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, could you clarify to the Trial Chamber, first of all, how -- what is the relationship between the MUP and the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The relationship between the MUP and the prison was such that certain relations were in place, because these are similar institutions but MUP was in charge of security and for combatting crimes; whereas, we, in prison, guarded the felons, tried to rehabilitate and reeducate them, et cetera. So once the MUP finish their part of job, they transfer them to judiciary, and we were the last link in this chain. So the very fact that the police had uniforms, that our guards had uniforms as well, that they were all armed with weapons and batons, the majority of citizens perceived them as police. They just didn't make any distinction. But in reality we were not together, and we did not belong to the same entity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So do I understand the position to be, Mr. Vidic, that the prison, in terms of the structure of government, that the prison was an autonomous agency and not subordinate to the MUP on the one hand, not subordinate to the Ministry of Justice. Do I get it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prison belonged to the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the warden and the prison guards were employees of the Ministry of Justice as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Ministry of Justice, there was a sector for law enforcement or execution of sanctions, and there was a judiciary section. The minister has an assistant for the execution of criminal sanctions, and he has another assistant for judicial affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I -- I'm sorry to -- to pick on this. But could I then revert to my original question. Why did you go to the MUP in order to resolve the problems or the situation that you found in the prison when you came that morning, on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to the MUP because my colleagues had told me that people in uniforms entered the building and locked up our three colleagues. That was the reason why I went to the MUP. I didn't go to the court because court had nothing to do with uniformed personnel. There were no uniformed personnel in court at the time. Nowadays, there are policemen in the court-house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. So what you understood when you came to the prison that morning on the 3rd of May was that the armed persons with camouflage paintings, that they were policemen rather than soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't think anything. In my view, they were only people in uniforms wearing arms. As to who they were, I didn't think anything at that particular moment. All I knew, that they were armed and they were dressed in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do I understand that you went to the MUP, which is the police, just because the police is the -- is the place to go when there is disturbance in the prison? As -- as a normal citizen would go to the police if there is any other disturbances in his house or something like that. You just went to the police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. I had no information whatsoever and that is why I went to the MUP, hoping to hearing is about the event from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to close this chapter before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, when you saw these people with camouflage uniforms, did you know which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Since upon my arrival in prison, I heard that our three Muslim employees had been incarcerated, it became clear to me that these men in uniform were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there any other distinctive feature about these men, besides the uniform and the paint on the face?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. It's difficult for me. Can you imagine how shocked you become if you enter such a room, and it really blurs your memory. All I wanted was to pass by those men as soon as I could. One of the men who was lying on the floor asked me, Who is this guy? And the other one responded, He works here. And I just went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And one last question before the break. Were they wearing any helmets or any other distinctive features?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: They had hats, they had caps, all of them made of camouflage material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What kind of hats are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Camouflage hats of the type that I hadn't seen before, except in films. That kind of hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May be a good time to take the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, I would like to take you back to the point where you told us that, on the 3rd of May, people were being brought into the prison. Could you tell us what you witnessed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: At first, I didn't see anything. When we were training to work in a penal/correctional facility and when we were passing specialized exams, we were learning how to work in normal conditions, so it came as a shock to me. I simply withdrew into my office, and I wasn't clear about what was going on. At that time, the greatest burden was on the guards. Later, when Slavuljica came, we had an opportunity to discuss. Something needed to be done; but what and how?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the people being brought in, can you tell us, on the 3rd of May and over the course of the next days, who was being brought in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: You mean in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's begin with that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: They were bringing in Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And these people -- these Muslims and Croats were from where exactly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: That's hard to say with any certainty. Because in those first days, they were brought without any papers, any documents, any warrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were these people from the municipality of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: That very first day, no. But, later on, I did recognise some. There were among them my former schoolmates, and also a former teacher of mine. Some of my work colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what were these people wearing, the people that were being brought into the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Although, later on, it was hard to say. Some were also brought wearing military uniforms. But in the first round, they were all wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the people who were bringing the people, who were they? Who were the people bringing in people in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. In those first days, we had absolutely no information. I just told you that Slavuljica and I discussed what to do, and how. At first, we were clueless.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I will not ask you any specific number at this stage. But could you give us, roughly speaking, the number of people that were being brought into the prison in those first few days, in the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you even a rough estimate. It would be pure speculation. But there were lists, and there are still lists. So everything is clear. Nothing was concealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We will look at those lists in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The witness answered your question as to who were bringing in the people, and the witness said that, At first they were clueless. That suggests at some point they did find out. Could you just finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, you heard Your Honour's [sic] question. Could you tell us eventually, if you found out, who were bringing prisoners in your prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. No, at first, we couldn't find out, because things were happening in the way they were happening. We, nevertheless, wanted to keep some sort of records, and we took a notebook and turned into a register, into which we entered the name and surname of the person who was brought in, the date and hour when they were brought, the date and hour of release. But, at first, we didn't know, and we never found out. Although, there were so many armed groups of all sorts. It was difficult to find out who they were. We never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Those armed groups that you're referring to eventually -- I know you said in the earlier days you didn't know. Did you eventually found out to which organisation they belonged to and who was bringing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you discover the purpose for which the detainees were brought in to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I thought you said that you registered them. So I assume that you must have had some conversations with them, with the detainees, as to why they were being detained. And were they detained against their will or for their protection? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not our job. We did not interview them. We did not inquire into that, and physically we were not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, were the prisoners brought in with the adequate paperwork for their detention, as was the case prior to the war? Were they brought in with the proper paperwork?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. At first, there was no paperwork at all. There was no warrant, no order sending these people to us. And, later on, I suppose that as we needed time, the police also needed time to consolidate. So, at a later stage, we did get warrants for detention. But those warrants were not filled in properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when these people were being brought in the prison, you told us that you have a duty officer at the entrance. Were you ever informed by the duty officer as to who was bringing these people in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You didn't ask who brought these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. There was no sense in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that you called Mirko Slavuljica and he arrived on the 3rd of May. Did he go back to the army reserve?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: He did not. Not until he left the prison for good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when did he leave the prison for good?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but it could have been between the 15th and the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after the 15th or the 20th of June, 1992, did somebody replace him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in those earlier days, did the prison administration - and by that I mean either Mr. Slavuljica or yourself - get into contact with the MUP, in relation to the numbers of prisoners being brought in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Slavuljica went to the MUP; I know that. And he had contacts there. But what he discussed, and with whom, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have discussions with him about going to speak to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did he tell you who he was planning to meet at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: What we discussed is -- is that something needed to be done, some steps needed to be made to restore some kind of normalcy in our work. And I know that, on one occasion, he went and talked to the chief of the centre because soon afterwards, a letter came from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you remember who was the chief of the centre at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Slavuljica tell to Andrija Bjelosevic? Did he tell you, or did you ever find out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: We had our discussions before that, that he should go to the MUP and try to see if it's possible at all to prevent these incursions by paramilitary groups into the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "incursions by paramilitary groups," what did you learn about these incursions? What happened exactly during those incursions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: They beat up prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how frequently did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say how often. We didn't count these raids, but we took steps after every raid. We heard from individuals that these raids usually happened after military clashes with the other side, with the enemy, when one of their fellow fighters were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that a letter came out from the centre. Was this after the meeting that Mr. Slavuljica had with Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How did Mr. Slavuljica approach this issue with Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Slavuljica just went to the MUP and talked to someone. I wasn't there; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Inside the prison you told us what the capacity was before the war. What was the situation after the 3rd of May, in terms of the capacity of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The question of capacity wasn't raised. Everyone brought in was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was this capacity respected after the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in relation to supplies, such as food, water, et cetera, what was the condition? What was the situation in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There were no conditions, as such. In the first few days, we had some food, and in the times of the state as existed previously, there was a rule that the prison had to have food supplies for at least ten days in case of emergencies, so that, in the first few days, the situation was relatively satisfactory. Sometimes the town bakery didn't work, and there was no bread in the town. Bread for the hospital was baked in the surrounding villages, and we had in prison, a sack of flour that Slavuljica used to ask a private baker to bake some bread. And, later on, when the supplies were as -- were exhausted, which happened quite quickly, we raided all the shops in Doboj and the food factory in Doboj. And as long as they had any reserves, they gave them to us. Later on, after the UNHCR came, the situation changed completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask for 65 ter 3530 to be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd like to you take a look at this document. It will appear in a moment. ? This is a document of the 12th of June, 1992, from the CSB Doboj. Could you, first of all, tell us if you've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you see it at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you please read the first paragraph, after it says: "Order."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: "I strictly prohibit arbitrary entry into the premises of the Doboj District Prison, and the rooms for temporary detention of persons in public security stations, as well as the use of physical intimidation and physical force against imprisoned and detained persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we scroll to the bottom of that page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you see there that it is signed by Andrija Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this the letter that you were referring to that came after Mr. Slavuljica met Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge - I know it's been 18 years - this document is issued on the 12th of June, roughly speaking, how much time before this order did Mr. Slavuljica met -- meet Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I can't say, but it was not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would ask -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the results of this order? Since it was issued by the CSB, I would assume that the police would then take action here, and seek to implement the order and prevent those armed incursions into the prison. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, you heard the question. What was the impact of this order?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago that the police also took time to consolidate just as we did. After this order came, some further raids happened, but nothing comparable to the state of affairs before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was this order publicised in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It was addressed by the CSB chief. To whom was it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I know it was sent to us. Whether it was sent to anyone else, I don't know. For a while, this order was on the desk of the duty officer at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, as a result of this order, did you -- you said that there was a change. Was there anybody to prevent those soldiers from entering the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But, to your knowledge, shortly after this document was issued, the incursions ceased?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not immediately, but they were reduced in scale. Sometime -- and it's hard to say exactly when, but I think the last raid happened in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, considering the that the witness had received the document at the time and he recognises it, may I ask for the document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, you mentioned to us that there were beatings inside the prison by the soldiers you described earlier. Were there any examples or any occurrences of beatings by members of other organisations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No, not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was there examples of prison guards beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: There was one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened to that case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: We had one guard who hailed from the area of Knin, and when there was a mass exodus of population from Knin, he came into the compound, took out a prisoner, and used physical force against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to that prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: The next morning, that prisoner was found dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what did you do about the guard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: He was suspended, and we informed the military court, because the military court became involved, and the prisoner was under the jurisdiction of the military court. We also informed the prosecutor's office and the MUP, and an order was given to conduct a post mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When did this happen? First of all, was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No. No, that was perhaps in the end of 1993 -- sorry, towards the end of 1992 or early 1993. I can't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Besides this guard, do you know if any measures were taken against the other persons who were beating prisoners inside the prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: We were not able to take any steps against any of the others who were members of paramilitary organisations. This one man was our own guard, and we did what we could against him, and what was our duty to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, I was just wondering about the information that the witness just gave to us. Namely, that the case was brought to the military court. Why was that? And not the civilian court and the civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We may have a document that will clarify this later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But right now, Mr. Vidic, if can you help the Trial Chamber understand why was the case of this guard taken before the military court?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Among all those people who had been brought in were a number of persons against whom criminal reports were filed within the basic court in Doboj and the other group of prisoners for whom reports were filed with the military court. So, therefore, we had both military and civilian prisoners. This particular prisoner that we just mentioned was captured as a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have some documents to clarify this later on with the criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, did there come a time when you met members of the Crisis Staff in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber in what circumstances you met with the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Once Slavuljica decided to leave the prison and join the army, he went to the Crisis Staff, and then after he came back, he told me that I was appointed commissioner. I asked Slavuljica whether there was any document to that effect, but he said there wasn't. There wasn't any decision or written decision. Due to that, I went to the Crisis Staff, where I was given a piece of paper on which it was written that I was appointed commissioner at the district prison in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who did you meet to receive this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: This piece of paper was given to me by Vlado Djurdjevic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was his function in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was he a member of any organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the document was signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: By himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when I was asking you about whether you met members of the Crisis Staff, are we to understand that this person was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. He was there in the building where the Crisis Staff was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And where was the building of the Crisis Staff headquartered?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: In the building of the railway transport company. It is situated across the street from the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would like for 65 ter 3538 to be displayed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, this document dated from the 15th of July, 1992, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the bottom of that page, please. I apologise, in the B/C/S version, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the header here says that it was addressed to the Presidency of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, Banja Luka. Can you please explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I can't. I can't. It was a long time ago. Probably we received this circular or letter from the Ministry of Justice. But why it all happened, it would be inappropriate for me to comment. Probably the new ministry instructed us to send this to the address that you see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, we do see here that Mr. Slavuljica, acting prison warden was an officer of Serbian army at the front. And we see next to your name the word "commissioner." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. By this time, Mr. Slavuljica was not at the prison anymore?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page in the B/C/S version; and in the English version, can we turn to page 3. And I refer to the paragraph beginning with: "Doboj district prison has been operating in wartime conditions since 3 May 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the second sentence, Mr. Vidic, which begins with: "Given the impossibility of contacting the Ministry of Justice ..."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you read the rest of that sentence to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: "Given the impossibility of contacting the Ministry of Justice, it has constantly worked in accordance with the regulations in force and the instructions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Doboj, although there are persons detained in part of the prison without a decision on detention."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, does this mean that there was still people detained without the adequate paperwork?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you go down to two paragraphs below the sentence beginning with: "For example on 30 May ..." Does it say that: "Food was provided for 500 persons," and currently for 550 persons along with the prison staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe to us who these 500 persons are.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm talking here about foodstuffs without mentioning either the number of employees or prisoners, et cetera. Again, I cannot give you any dates, but for a period of time we prepared and cooked food for the police. Since we were one among the few institutions in this compound that had a cauldron for cooking large quantities of food. So for a short period of time we provided them with meals, but who exactly these meals went to, we didn't know exactly, whether it went to the military barracks in Bare, actually. I don't know. Later on, there were some detainees at Usora as well, but none of our personnel was there. We only provided food for that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Therefore, you are not able to tell us what is -- what are those 500 persons exactly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. Except for those who were there in the prison and the prison staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page of this document in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The first line of the document reads: "Regarding the circular by the Ministry of Justice, number 01/2-3/92." Is it the case that you were replying to a request from the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1306, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we display now 65 ter 3534.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What is the reference number on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VIDIC
utterances.text: 13th of February, 1992.
